courses.summary: The ideal first step: learn the Arabic letters, their correct sounds and the basic rules you need to read the Quran.
courses.description_html:
Noorani Qaida is the classic foundation for reading the Quran. Your teacher starts with the Arabic letters and their correct articulation points (makharij), then builds step by step to joined letters, vowels, long vowels and the first Tajweed rules — until you can read complete verses with confidence.

Who is it for?

Complete beginners with no Arabic background: children from about 4½–5 years old, and adults who want to learn to read from scratch or correct their pronunciation.

How classes work

Every lesson is live and one-to-one. No physical book is needed — your teacher shows a digital Qaida on screen, and PDF copies are shared for practice at home. Female and male teachers are available.

How long does it take?

Children taking three classes a week usually finish in about four to six months. Adults often progress faster, depending on practice time.

courses.summary: Memorise the Quran with a structured Sabaq, Sabqi and Manzil revision system and regular oral assessments.
courses.description_html:
Our Hifz programme combines traditional recitation methods, proven memorisation techniques and a disciplined revision system. Each student follows a personal plan — the whole Quran, a particular Juz, or selected surahs.

Who is it for?

Children and adults who have completed Noorani Qaida (or equivalent) and can read Arabic correctly with basic Tajweed. You do not need to speak Arabic. Beginners should start with Noorani Qaida or Nazara first.

The three-part revision system

  • Sabaq — the new lesson, recited daily.
  • Sabqi — revision of the last seven days of memorisation.
  • Manzil — a steady rotation through everything memorised earlier.

Routine oral assessments keep memorisation strong and accurate.

How long does it take?

Memorising the whole Quran typically takes two to four years, depending on ability, class frequency and revision at home.

posts.title: How to Help Your Kids Learn Quran Online Successfully
posts.excerpt: Online Quran classes work brilliantly for children when parents set up a few simple habits. Here is a practical checklist for families.
posts.body_html:
Learning the Quran online gives children something many families could never arrange locally: a dedicated teacher, one-to-one attention and classes that fit around school and family life. A few simple habits at home make the difference between a child who logs in and a child who truly flourishes.

1. Make a calm, regular learning corner

Choose a quiet spot with good light, away from the television and siblings' games. Keep the device charged, the camera at eye level and headphones ready. When the corner is used only for learning, children settle into the lesson faster.

2. Keep the same days and times every week

Consistency matters more than long lessons. Three short classes a week at fixed times usually beats one long class. Put the schedule on the fridge and treat class time like a school lesson.

3. Join the first few minutes

Especially for younger children, sit nearby at the start of class. You will see how the teacher works, and your child feels supported. Gradually step back as they grow in confidence.

4. Practise for ten minutes a day

A short daily practice — revising the last lesson from the Qaida or reciting a memorised surah — keeps what was learned fresh. Little and often is the secret to steady progress.

5. Talk to the teacher

Share what motivates your child, what they find difficult and any changes at home. Ask how you can help between classes. Teachers and parents working together is the strongest combination.

6. Celebrate effort, not just results

Praise your child for trying, for sitting well and for revising without being asked. Mark milestones such as finishing the Qaida or memorising a new surah with something special.

7. Make the Quran part of family life

Children copy what they see. Reciting together after Fajr or before bed, listening to recitation in the car and talking about the meaning of short surahs all show that the Quran is part of everyday life — not just a lesson.

The Prophet ﷺ said: “The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it” (Sahih al-Bukhari). With patience, routine and encouragement, online classes can help your child begin that journey with joy.

posts.title: The Importance of Reciting Quran with Tajweed
posts.excerpt: Tajweed protects the meaning of the Quran and beautifies its recitation. Here is what it is, why it matters and how to start learning it.
posts.body_html:
Tajweed comes from an Arabic root meaning “to make better” or “to perfect”. In recitation it means giving every letter its right: pronouncing it from its correct place of articulation, with its correct qualities, and applying the rules that govern how letters affect one another.

Why Tajweed matters

It protects the meaning

Arabic letters that sound similar to a beginner can completely change a word's meaning. Learning correct pronunciation ensures that what we recite is what was revealed.

It follows the way the Quran was taught

The Quran was passed down orally, teacher to student, with its precise recitation. Allah says: “…and recite the Quran with measured recitation” (Al-Muzzammil 73:4). Learning Tajweed connects us to that living chain of teaching.

It beautifies recitation and deepens focus

When recitation is steady and correct, it becomes easier to reflect, to feel the rhythm of the verses and to concentrate in salah.

Key areas you will learn

  • Makharij — the points of articulation for each letter.
  • Sifat — the qualities of letters, such as heaviness and lightness.
  • Rules of noon sakinah and tanween — izhar, idgham, iqlab and ikhfa.
  • Madd — lengthening vowels for the correct count.
  • Waqf — where and how to stop and start.

How to start

Tajweed is learned best by listening and correction, which is why one-to-one classes are so effective: your teacher hears every letter and corrects it immediately. Beginners start with Noorani Qaida; those who can already read move to Nazara, where Tajweed rules are applied in real recitation.

Start small, practise daily and be patient. Every improvement in recitation is an investment that stays with you for life.

posts.title: Effective Memorization Techniques for Beginners
posts.excerpt: Starting Hifz? These proven techniques — chunking, consistent Mushaf, daily routine and the Sabaq-Sabqi-Manzil cycle — help memorisation stick.
posts.body_html:
Memorising the Quran is one of the most rewarding journeys a Muslim can take. Whether you are aiming for the whole Quran or a few surahs from Juz Amma, the right method makes progress steady and lasting.

1. Read correctly before you memorise

Memorise only what you can already read accurately with Tajweed. Mistakes memorised early are hard to remove later, so ask your teacher to check your recitation first.

2. Learn in small chunks

Break the lesson into single verses or short phrases. Repeat each part until it flows, then join it to the previous part. Daily goals of three to five lines are realistic for most beginners.

3. Use the same Mushaf every time

Your memory links each verse to its place on the page. Using one consistent Mushaf layout turns that visual memory into a powerful tool.

4. Follow the Sabaq, Sabqi and Manzil cycle

  • Sabaq — the new lesson for today.
  • Sabqi — revision of what you memorised in the last week.
  • Manzil — a regular rotation through everything memorised earlier.

New memorisation without revision fades quickly; this cycle keeps everything strong.

5. Choose the best time of day

Many students find the time after Fajr the most focused. Whatever time you choose, keep it the same each day.

6. Listen and recite aloud

Listen to a trusted reciter, then recite aloud yourself. Recording your own recitation and comparing it can reveal small errors.

7. Understand what you memorise

Knowing the meaning of a verse makes it easier to remember and far more meaningful in salah.

8. Recite to a teacher regularly

A teacher hears what you cannot: a missed letter, a skipped word, a rule not applied. Regular recitation to a teacher, plus routine oral assessments, keeps your Hifz accurate.

Above all, be consistent and make dua for ease. Small daily steps, kept up over months and years, achieve remarkable things.

Online Quran College (“we”, “us”) is committed to handling the personal data of our website visitors, students and parents safely and responsibly. This policy explains what we collect and why.

  • To arrange trial classes, enrolment and class schedules.
  • To communicate with you about lessons, progress and administration.
  • To provide support and handle requests or complaints.
  • To improve our website and courses.

3. Sharing and security

We do not sell, trade or rent your personal information. Access is limited to staff who need it for their role, and we use appropriate security measures to protect it. No method of transmission over the internet is completely secure, but we work hard to keep your data safe.

4. Cookies

You may ask to access, correct or delete your personal data at any time by emailing info@onlinequrancollege.com.

6. Changes to this policy

We may update this policy from time to time. The latest version will always be published on this page.

7. Contact

Online Quran College, United Kingdom · info@onlinequrancollege.com · +44 7864 710821

Campaign attribution and browser storage

When a website link includes campaign tags (utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term or utm_content) or click identifiers (gclid or fbclid), we keep those values and the landing-page path in this tab’s sessionStorage under oqc-campaign. Browser attribution is used for up to 24 hours after the most recent tagged visit and is normally cleared when the tab closes. An expired entry is removed the next time attribution is checked. A new tagged visit replaces the earlier campaign. Forms still work when this browser storage is blocked.

If you submit an enquiry, campaign details are included with that enquiry for staff reporting. The 24-hour browser limit does not delete a submitted enquiry from our records. You can contact us to ask about access, correction or deletion of your enquiry data.

Website chat

The website chat feature loads a third-party script from app.hatchium.ai, provided by Hatchium. Messages and contact details you enter in chat are handled by Hatchium to provide the conversation service. Ask the college if you have questions about how your chat data is handled.

Website enquiry forms are stored in the college CMS. Automatic forwarding of those forms to Make or the chat service is not currently enabled. We do not automatically copy website form fields into chat.
